client: I've been really struggling since my grandfather passed away a few weeks ago, and with my final exams starting next week, I just can't seem to focus on anything. Every time I sit down to study, I end up just staring at the wall or thinking about him, and then I feel this crushing weight that makes it impossible to get anything done. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help me pass my exams or bring him back, so I don't really know what I'm doing here.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is so heavy — grief and pressure colliding at the worst possible time, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps drifting to your grandfather instead of your textbooks. I also hear a kind of quiet exhaustion in what you're sharing, like you're running on empty and maybe even a little unsure whether you deserve to slow down and feel this. You don't have to have a clear reason for being here — sometimes just putting words to the weight is the first small step, and I'm glad you came.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I guess that's part of it — I keep feeling like I shouldn't be falling apart right now, like I should just push through and deal with the grief later when exams are over. But then I sit down with my notes and I just feel this wave of guilt, like studying feels almost disrespectful to his memory somehow, like I'm supposed to be mourning more fully or something. It's this weird loop where I can't really do either thing properly.
therapist: That loop you're describing — where grief blocks studying and studying triggers guilt — is such a painful place to be stuck, and it makes a lot of sense given how much you loved him. I'm curious, though: you're speaking quite quickly, like there's a lot of pressure building up inside as you describe this — do you notice that urgency in your body too, almost like you're racing against something? It might be worth gently exploring whether part of you believes that if you slow down and actually feel the grief, something will fall apart completely.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think that's probably true — like if I actually let myself sit with how much I miss him, I'll just completely break down and then I definitely won't be able to study at all, and everything will fall apart right before these exams. It's almost easier to stay in this anxious, half-functional state than to risk fully feeling it. But I don't really see how slowing down and exploring that is going to help me get through next week practically speaking.
therapist: What you just described is actually a really important insight — that staying anxious feels *safer* than risking a full breakdown, which is a kind of protection your mind has built to keep you functioning, even if it's exhausting. The CBT perspective here is that our brains often overestimate how catastrophic it would be to fully feel something, and that the "controlled breakdown" we fear rarely looks as devastating as we imagine. I wonder, has there been a moment recently, even briefly, where you did let yourself feel the grief a little — and what actually happened?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: There was one moment a few days ago when I found one of his old voicemails on my phone, and I just started crying really hard for maybe ten or fifteen minutes. And honestly, I did feel a little lighter afterward, not fixed or anything, but like the pressure in my chest had gone down slightly. But I guess I'm scared that was just a coincidence, or that if I try to intentionally let myself feel it, it won't work the same way and I'll just be stuck in the middle of it with no way out.
therapist: That moment with the voicemail is actually really significant evidence against the story your mind is telling you — you let yourself feel it, and you didn't fall apart permanently, you came through the other side feeling lighter. The fear that it "won't work" if it's intentional is so common, but grief doesn't really follow those rules — your nervous system needed that release, and it responded, and that's not a coincidence. What do you think your grandfather would have wanted for you this week — the crushing, frozen version of you, or the one who lets himself cry for fifteen minutes and then keeps going?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stops me, because I know the answer — he would have hated seeing me like this, frozen and miserable. He was always the type to say you have to keep living, he was pretty practical about that stuff. But it still feels a bit manipulative as a technique, like you're using him to get me to do something, and I'm not sure I'm comfortable with that even if the logic makes sense.
therapist: That's a completely fair pushback, and I actually respect that you named it — your instinct to question the techniques being used on you is healthy, not resistant. You're right that I was using something meaningful to you to make a point, and it's worth you knowing that you're always in the driver's seat here, not being steered somewhere without your consent. What feels more genuine to you — what *you* know about what he'd want, separate from any technique I might use?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I take the technique out of it, I do know he would have wanted me to get through these exams — he was really proud of me being in school and used to ask about my grades all the time. That part feels true in a way that isn't just me being talked into something. I guess I'm just not sure how to hold both things at once, like actually grieving him and still functioning, because it feels like they're pulling in opposite directions.
therapist: What you just said — that it feels true in a way that isn't you being talked into something — that's really worth holding onto, because it means you're starting to trust your own knowing rather than needing me to lead you there. The idea that grieving and functioning are opposites is one of the most common and painful myths about loss, but your experience with the voicemail already showed you they can coexist — fifteen minutes of tears, then a little more room to breathe. What might it look like to build in small, intentional spaces for grief this week, rather than trying to keep the lid on it entirely while you study?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think maybe I could try setting aside like twenty minutes in the evening to look at some photos of him or something, just a dedicated time where I let myself feel it instead of it ambushing me while I'm trying to study. But I'm worried that twenty minutes won't feel like enough, or that I'll look at the clock and feel like I'm putting a timer on my grief, which seems kind of cold and clinical. I don't know, maybe the structure would help but it also feels a bit artificial.
therapist: The fact that you came up with that idea yourself is really meaningful — it shows a part of you already knows what you need, even if another part is second-guessing it. The structure isn't about putting a cold timer on grief, it's more like creating a container so the grief has somewhere to go instead of leaking into everything else, which is actually a way of taking it seriously. And if twenty minutes turns into thirty, or you close the photos early, that's okay too — you're allowed to let it be flexible and human rather than perfectly clinical.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: The "container" framing actually makes it feel a bit less cold to me, like I'm making space for him rather than scheduling him in between other tasks. I think I could try it, maybe starting tonight actually. I'm still worried about the exams though, because even if the grief piece gets a little better, I've genuinely lost a lot of study time and I'm not sure feeling emotionally lighter is going to fix that practical problem.
therapist: It's really good that you're thinking about starting tonight — that's you moving from insight into action, which is often the hardest step. Your concern about lost study time is completely legitimate and worth taking seriously, so it might help to think practically about what's actually still possible between now and the exams, rather than measuring yourself against the study plan you had before your grandfather died. What would "good enough" preparation look like given everything you're carrying right now, rather than the version you'd planned in a different life?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That question is actually kind of a relief to hear, because I've been holding myself to this original study plan like it's still the only valid version of success, and that's been making everything feel even more impossible. I think "good enough" right now might just be getting through the key topics instead of every single detail, and maybe accepting that a B is okay when a few weeks ago I was aiming for an A. It's hard to let go of that standard though, because part of me feels like lowering the bar is just giving up, and I don't want to use grief as an excuse to underperform.
therapist: There's an important distinction worth sitting with here — adjusting your standards in response to genuinely extraordinary circumstances isn't giving up, it's accurate thinking about what's actually possible, which is very different from making excuses. A B while grieving your grandfather during finals week might actually represent more resilience and effort than an A would have before any of this happened. What do you think it would mean about you as a person if you got a B this semester — is the fear really about the grade, or about what you're afraid it says about you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think honestly the fear is that it says I'm not as capable as I've been telling myself, like the grades have been this proof that I'm good enough and smart enough, and without that I'm not sure what I'm left with. My grandfather actually believed in me so much, and part of me feels like getting lower grades now that he's gone would somehow confirm that I needed his belief to prop me up. That's a pretty uncomfortable thing to realize out loud.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that the grades haven't just been about achievement, they've been evidence you've been collecting to prove your own worth to yourself. The fear isn't really about a B, it's about whether you're enough without the external proof, and that's a question worth sitting with gently rather than trying to answer with exam results. I'm curious — whose voice is it that originally told you that you needed to keep proving yourself like this, and was it ever actually your grandfather's?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
